accepted_variants: The vector r specifying location relative to an origin.
cards.definition: A position vector points from a chosen origin to a particle's location. Its components depend on the coordinate system and can vary with time.
major_error_concepts: Treating position as independent of the chosen origin.
cards.prompt: What is Position Vector? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Vector from chosen origin to particle.
Coordinates depend on the reference choice.

accepted_variants: Instantaneous vector rate of change of location.
cards.definition: Instantaneous velocity is the time derivative of position, v = dr/dt. It points tangent to the trajectory, and its magnitude is speed.
major_error_concepts: Treating speed and velocity as identical vector quantities.
cards.prompt: What is Velocity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Time derivative of position.
Speed is the magnitude of velocity.

accepted_variants: Instantaneous vector rate of velocity change.
cards.definition: Acceleration is the time derivative of velocity, a = dv/dt. It can arise from a change in speed, direction, or both; constant speed does not imply zero acceleration.
major_error_concepts: Claiming uniform circular motion has zero acceleration because speed is constant.
cards.prompt: What is Acceleration? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Derivative of velocity.
Directional change also produces acceleration.

accepted_variants: The proportionality between net force and acceleration.
cards.definition: Inertial mass measures a body's resistance to acceleration under a given net force. In Newtonian mechanics with constant mass, a = F_net/m; mass is a scalar property distinct from weight.
major_error_concepts: Measuring mass in newtons or treating it as location-dependent weight.
cards.prompt: What is Inertial Mass? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Mass sets response to net force.
Mass differs from gravitational force or weight.

accepted_variants: The location R defined by the first spatial mass moment divided by total mass.
cards.definition: The center of mass is the mass-weighted mean position: R = sum(m_i r_i)/M, with an integral for continuous matter. It can lie outside the material of the object.
major_error_concepts: Taking an unweighted position average when masses differ.
cards.prompt: What is Center of Mass? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Mass-weighted average position.
Need not coincide with a material point or geometric center.

cards.definition: A rigid body is an idealization in which distances between all pairs of material points remain constant. It can translate and rotate but cannot deform within the model.
major_error_concepts: Confusing rigidity with being fixed in place.
cards.prompt: What is Rigid Body? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Internal pairwise distances are fixed.
Translation and rotation remain possible.

cards.definition: Linear momentum of a Newtonian particle is p = m v. It is a vector and the momentum of a system is the vector sum of its constituents' momenta.
major_error_concepts: Equating momentum with the scalar kinetic energy.
cards.prompt: What is Linear Momentum? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: p equals mass times velocity.
System momentum is a vector sum.

accepted_variants: Energy associated with particle motion in a specified frame.
cards.definition: The translational kinetic energy of a Newtonian particle is K = one-half m v squared. It is nonnegative and depends on the reference frame through speed.
major_error_concepts: Assigning negative kinetic energy merely because velocity is negative.
cards.prompt: What is Kinetic Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: K = m v squared divided by two.
Scalar and frame-dependent.

accepted_variants: Energy function whose negative gradient generates the conservative force.
cards.definition: A conservative force admits a potential energy U such that its work equals -delta U. Equivalently F = -gradient U where the potential is differentiable; the additive zero of U is arbitrary.
major_error_concepts: Using F = positive gradient U.
Assuming potential energy must always be nonnegative.
cards.prompt: What is Potential Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Conservative work equals negative potential-energy change.
Only potential differences matter to the force.

cards.definition: Torque about a chosen origin is tau = r cross F, where r points from that origin to the force's application point. Its magnitude is force times perpendicular lever arm; its direction follows the right-hand rule.
major_error_concepts: Using the full distance as lever arm regardless of force direction.
cards.prompt: What is Torque? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Cross product relative to a specified origin.
Use perpendicular lever arm.

accepted_variants: Rotational inertia about a specified axis.
cards.definition: Moment of inertia about an axis is I = sum m_i r_perp,i squared, or its continuous integral. It depends on both the mass distribution and the chosen axis and measures resistance to angular acceleration about that axis.
major_error_concepts: Treating moment of inertia as a property independent of the axis.
cards.prompt: What is Moment of Inertia? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Mass weighted by squared perpendicular distance to the axis.
Axis-dependent.

cards.definition: A particle's angular momentum about an origin is L = r cross p. A system's angular momentum is the sum of these contributions; for rotation about a fixed principal axis its axial component is I omega.
major_error_concepts: Assuming L is always parallel to angular velocity for an arbitrary rigid-body rotation.
cards.prompt: What is Angular Momentum? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Origin-dependent cross product r cross p.
I omega is an appropriate axial special case, not an unrestricted vector identity.

cards.definition: Newton's universal gravitational force between point masses is attractive, has magnitude G m1 m2/r squared, and acts along the line joining them. The same exterior result applies to spherically symmetric masses treated from outside.
major_error_concepts: Applying the exterior point-mass formula inside every extended mass distribution without modification.
cards.prompt: What is Universal Gravitation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Inverse-square attractive force proportional to both masses.
Separation is between point masses or spherical centers in the appropriate case.

cards.definition: Constraint forces maintain imposed geometric conditions such as fixed string length or contact with a surface. Their allowed directions follow the constraint model: an ideal smooth surface supplies a normal reaction and a taut ideal string pulls along itself.
major_error_concepts: Choosing a convenient constraint-force direction unrelated to the actual surface or connector.
cards.prompt: What is Constraint Forces? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Geometry determines allowed force directions.
Force magnitude must satisfy dynamics and constraints together.

accepted_variants: The integrated kinetic-energy form of Newton's second law.
cards.definition: The work-energy theorem states that net work on a constant-mass particle equals its kinetic-energy change: W_net = delta K. It includes work by both conservative and nonconservative forces.
major_error_concepts: Equating net work with total mechanical-energy change in every situation.
cards.prompt: What is Work–Energy Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Net work equals kinetic-energy change.
All force contributions to work are included.

accepted_variants: Delta K + delta U = 0 for the conservative system.
cards.definition: Mechanical energy K + U is conserved when all working interactions in the model are conservative and no unaccounted energy transfer crosses the system boundary. Kinetic and potential energy can change individually while their sum remains fixed.
major_error_concepts: Imposing mechanical-energy conservation across a dissipative collision without accounting for internal energy.
cards.prompt: What is Mechanical-Energy Conservation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Conservative interactions and appropriate system boundary.
Conserved sum does not require K and U individually constant.

accepted_variants: Since dP/dt = F_external,net, P is constant when the external resultant vanishes at every time; equal and opposite impulses at different times only restore the original P afterward.
cards.definition: For a fixed Newtonian system in an inertial frame, total linear momentum remains constant throughout an interval if the net external force is zero throughout that interval. More generally, the momentum change equals external impulse. Zero impulse over one selected interval guarantees equal initial and final momenta, not constancy at every intermediate time. Internal interactions may redistribute momentum among constituents.
major_error_concepts: Claiming that canceling external impulses at different times imply momentum never changed in between.
Concluding each constituent's momentum is separately conserved during an isolated collision.
cards.prompt: What is Momentum Conservation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Zero net external force throughout the interval keeps total momentum constant for a fixed system in an inertial frame.
Zero net impulse over only the whole interval guarantees endpoint equality; individual constituents may still change momentum.

accepted_variants: The center of mass moves as a point particle under the resultant external force.
cards.definition: For a constant-total-mass Newtonian system, M a_CM = F_external,net. Internal interactions affect relative motion but cancel in the center-of-mass translational equation under the usual action-reaction assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Treating internal muscular forces as sufficient to accelerate an isolated person's center of mass.
cards.prompt: What is Center-of-Mass Dynamics? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Total mass times center-of-mass acceleration equals net external force.
Internal forces do not independently accelerate the system center of mass.

accepted_variants: Fixed-axis rotational form of Newtonian dynamics.
cards.definition: For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis with constant moment of inertia, the net torque component about that axis equals I alpha. Torques and inertia must refer to the same axis.
major_error_concepts: Combining torque about one axis with inertia about another.
cards.prompt: What is Fixed-Axis Rotational Dynamics? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Net axial torque equals I alpha.
Fixed axis and constant I.

cards.definition: Work in fixed-axis rotation is W = integral tau_axis d theta. For constant axial torque this is tau delta theta, and instantaneous power is tau omega.
major_error_concepts: Multiplying torque by angular velocity and calling the result work rather than power.
cards.prompt: What is Rotational Work? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Torque integrated over angular displacement.
Angular displacement uses radians.

cards.definition: The kinetic energy of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis is K_rot = one-half I omega squared. The chosen moment of inertia must be about that axis.
major_error_concepts: Using mass alone in place of moment of inertia.
cards.prompt: What is Rotational Kinetic Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: K_rot = I omega squared divided by two.
Inertia and angular speed describe the same rotation axis.

accepted_variants: The inertia shift formula for a parallel displaced axis.
cards.definition: The parallel-axis theorem states I = I_CM + M d squared for an axis parallel to one through the center of mass, with perpendicular separation d. One of the paired axes must be the center-of-mass axis in this form.
major_error_concepts: Applying the formula to nonparallel axes.
cards.prompt: What is Parallel-Axis Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: I equals I_CM plus M d squared.
Axes parallel, with one through the center of mass.

accepted_variants: A one-dimensional radial potential incorporating conserved angular motion.
cards.definition: For central-force motion with conserved angular momentum magnitude L, radial motion can be described using an effective potential U_eff(r) = U(r) + L squared/(2 m r squared). The second term represents the angular-motion energy in the reduced radial problem.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting the effective term as an additional fundamental outward interaction.
cards.prompt: What is Effective Potential? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Central-force reduction with fixed L.
Effective potential includes the positive angular-momentum barrier.

accepted_variants: No preferred absolute position implies the corresponding conserved momentum component under Noether's assumptions.
cards.definition: In a standard Lagrangian system, invariance under continuous spatial translations is associated through Noether's theorem with conserved total linear momentum. The symmetry must apply to the full modeled system, not just one part in an external position-dependent field.
major_error_concepts: Inferring momentum conservation despite a translation-breaking external potential.
cards.prompt: What is Translation Symmetry and Momentum? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Spatial translation symmetry corresponds to momentum conservation.
Symmetry is a property of the full dynamics.

accepted_variants: Time-independent dynamics admit an associated conserved energy under the usual Noether conditions.
cards.definition: In a standard Lagrangian system, continuous time-translation invariance is associated with conserved energy. An explicitly time-dependent external drive can break this symmetry for the subsystem and exchange energy with it.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a periodically driven subsystem must conserve its own mechanical energy.
cards.prompt: What is Time Symmetry and Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Time-translation symmetry corresponds to energy conservation.
External time-dependent driving changes the subsystem accounting.

accepted_variants: No preferred rotational orientation implies a Noether angular momentum.
cards.definition: In a standard Lagrangian system, continuous rotational symmetry corresponds to conservation of the associated angular-momentum component. Full spatial rotational symmetry gives conservation of the angular-momentum vector under the relevant assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Equating symmetry of an object's shape alone with symmetry of all forces acting on it.
cards.prompt: What is Rotational Symmetry and Angular Momentum? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Rotational invariance gives angular-momentum conservation.
Axis-specific symmetry conserves the corresponding component.

accepted_variants: Frame changes alter coordinate equations, not the underlying event.
cards.definition: The same motion can be described in inertial or accelerating coordinates. In an accelerating frame, velocity and acceleration transformations introduce inertial terms; including them consistently reproduces the inertial-frame predictions for physical observations.
major_error_concepts: Adding fictitious forces in an inertial frame while also keeping the original force equation.
cards.prompt: What is Inertial and Accelerating Descriptions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: One physical motion admits different frame descriptions.
Accelerating-frame equations need the appropriate inertial terms.

accepted_variants: The outward centrifugal pseudo-force of rotating coordinates.
cards.definition: In a frame rotating with angular velocity Omega, the centrifugal inertial force is -m Omega cross (Omega cross r). It points away from the rotation axis with magnitude m Omega squared times perpendicular distance for uniform rotation.
major_error_concepts: Replacing the actual inward centripetal resultant with an outward force in the inertial frame.
cards.prompt: What is Centrifugal Force? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Outward rotating-frame inertial term.
Not an extra real interaction in the inertial-frame description.

accepted_variants: The Coriolis pseudo-force caused by motion within a rotating frame.
cards.definition: The Coriolis inertial force in a frame rotating with angular velocity Omega is -2m Omega cross v_relative. It depends on motion relative to the rotating frame and is perpendicular to that relative velocity.
major_error_concepts: Assigning a nonzero Coriolis force to a body at rest in the rotating frame.
cards.prompt: What is Coriolis Force? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Velocity-dependent rotating-frame term.
Use velocity relative to the rotating coordinates.

accepted_variants: Potential minima are locally stable in the conservative one-dimensional setting.
cards.definition: In one-dimensional conservative motion, an equilibrium satisfies U'(x0) = 0. Positive second derivative gives a local potential minimum and local stability; negative second derivative gives instability. Zero curvature requires higher-order analysis.
major_error_concepts: Calling every zero-curvature equilibrium stable or unstable without further information.
cards.prompt: What is Potential Curvature and Stability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Equilibrium at zero first derivative.
Positive curvature stable, negative unstable, zero inconclusive.

cards.definition: Generalized coordinates are independent parameters that specify a system's configuration after applicable constraints are incorporated. They may be angles, lengths, or other variables, and need not be Cartesian position components.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every generalized coordinate must have units of length.
cards.prompt: What is Generalized Coordinates? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Independent configuration parameters consistent with constraints.

cards.definition: Degrees of freedom count the independent configuration parameters needed to specify the modeled system locally. For regular independent holonomic constraints, each constraint removes one configuration degree, but redundant constraints must not be counted twice.
major_error_concepts: Subtracting every written constraint without checking redundancy.
cards.prompt: What is Degrees of Freedom? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Number of independent configuration coordinates.
Only independent regular constraints reduce the count directly.

cards.definition: A holonomic constraint can be written as an equation among coordinates and possibly time, f(q,t)=0. When independent and regular it can be incorporated by reducing the configuration coordinates.
major_error_concepts: Calling every velocity constraint holonomic without establishing an equivalent coordinate relation.
cards.prompt: What is Holonomic Constraint? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Coordinate-and-time equation without essential velocity dependence.

accepted_variants: Velocity constraint not reducible to a holonomic relation.
cards.definition: A nonholonomic constraint cannot be reduced to the specified form of coordinate-only equality constraints, often because it restricts velocities in a nonintegrable way. Rolling constraints require examining the actual geometry rather than classifying all rolling identically.
major_error_concepts: Applying unrestricted coordinate elimination to every rolling constraint without checking integrability.
cards.prompt: What is Nonholonomic Constraint? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Nonintegrable restrictions beyond coordinate-only equalities.

cards.definition: A time-dependent constraint changes its allowed configuration set explicitly with time, such as a prescribed moving support. Constraint forces can then transfer energy even when the constraint is ideal in the virtual-work sense.
major_error_concepts: Assuming ideal moving constraints can never exchange energy with the system.
cards.prompt: What is Time-Dependent Constraint? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Allowed configuration relation depends explicitly on time.
Ideal constraints can still do actual work.

cards.definition: A virtual displacement is an infinitesimal change between configurations compatible with the constraints at a fixed time. It differs from an actual displacement during elapsed time, especially for moving constraints.
major_error_concepts: Including prescribed time evolution in a virtual displacement while claiming time is held fixed.
cards.prompt: What is Virtual Displacement? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Constraint-compatible variation at fixed time.

cards.definition: An ideal constraint has reaction forces whose total virtual work vanishes for admissible virtual displacements. This property does not necessarily imply zero work along actual motion when the constraints depend on time.
major_error_concepts: Equating zero virtual work with zero actual work for all moving constraints.
cards.prompt: What is Ideal Constraint? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Reaction forces do zero admissible virtual work.

cards.definition: D'Alembert's principle states that the total virtual work of applied forces minus inertial terms m a vanishes for admissible virtual displacements under ideal constraints. It turns dynamics into a virtual-work statement without asserting the body is at rest.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting D'Alembert's principle as ordinary static force balance with zero acceleration.
cards.prompt: What is D'Alembert Principle? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Sum of applied-minus-inertial force virtual work equals zero.

cards.definition: A generalized force Q_j is defined through virtual work as delta W=sum Q_j delta q_j. For particle forces, Q_j=sum F_i dot partial r_i/partial q_j, so its units depend on the coordinate.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every generalized force has units of newtons even for angular coordinates.
cards.prompt: What is Generalized Force? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Force coefficient conjugate to generalized displacement in virtual work.

cards.definition: For a standard mechanical system with conservative position-dependent forces, the Lagrangian is L=T-U expressed in generalized coordinates and velocities. More general Lagrangians can include velocity dependence beyond the usual kinetic term.
major_error_concepts: Using T+U as the ordinary conservative mechanical Lagrangian.
cards.prompt: What is Lagrangian? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Standard Lagrangian T minus U.
Generalized coordinates and velocities are its variables.

cards.definition: The action is the time integral of a Lagrangian along a trial configuration path. It is a functional of the whole path, not simply the energy at one instant.
major_error_concepts: Equating action with instantaneous energy.
cards.prompt: What is Action Functional? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Integral of L over a path's time interval.

cards.definition: Hamilton's principle requires the action to be stationary under admissible path variations with fixed endpoints in the standard formulation. Stationary need not mean a minimum; maxima or saddle behavior can occur in variational problems.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every physical path globally minimizes action over every possible path.
cards.prompt: What is Stationary Action Principle? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: First variation of action vanishes with appropriate fixed endpoints.

cards.definition: The Euler-Lagrange equation is d/dt(partial L/partial qdot_j)-partial L/partial q_j=0 for the standard unforced variational problem. Applied nonconservative generalized forces can appear on the right under the appropriate formulation.
major_error_concepts: Omitting the time derivative on partial L/partial qdot.
cards.prompt: What is Euler-Lagrange Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Correct time derivative and coordinate derivative combination.

accepted_variants: Equivalent Lagrangians up to a total derivative.
cards.definition: Adding a total time derivative dF(q,t)/dt to a Lagrangian leaves its Euler-Lagrange trajectories unchanged for fixed endpoint variations. The action changes by an endpoint term, and canonical momenta or energy expressions can change representation.
major_error_concepts: Assuming equivalent Lagrangians must have identical canonical momentum formulas.
cards.prompt: What is Total-Derivative Lagrangian Freedom? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Total derivative changes only endpoint action contribution.
Equations remain unchanged under standard endpoint conditions.

cards.definition: A cyclic coordinate does not appear explicitly in the Lagrangian, so its conjugate momentum is conserved when no corresponding nonconservative generalized force acts. Its velocity may still appear in L.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a cyclic coordinate's velocity must be zero.
cards.prompt: What is Cyclic Coordinate? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: No explicit q dependence implies conserved conjugate momentum under stated conditions.

cards.definition: The generalized momentum conjugate to q_j is p_j=partial L/partial qdot_j. It equals an ordinary linear momentum component only in suitable coordinates and models, not universally.
major_error_concepts: Replacing every generalized momentum by m qdot without considering coordinates or velocity-dependent interactions.
cards.prompt: What is Generalized Momentum? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Velocity derivative of L.
Need not equal mass times generalized velocity.

cards.definition: Noether's theorem associates continuous variational symmetries of an action with conserved quantities under the applicable equations and boundary assumptions. A conserved component follows from the corresponding symmetry, not merely from a visually symmetric trajectory.
major_error_concepts: Inferring a conserved quantity from a subsystem symmetry that is broken by its external forcing.
cards.prompt: What is Noether Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Continuous action symmetry implies a conservation law.

cards.definition: The Lagrangian energy function is E_L=sum qdot_j p_j-L. Along unforced Euler-Lagrange motion its time derivative is minus the explicit partial derivative of L with respect to time, so an autonomous L gives a conserved E_L.
major_error_concepts: Equating any time-independent Lagrangian energy function with T+U without checking its form.
cards.prompt: What is Lagrangian Energy Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: E_L=sum velocity times conjugate momentum minus L.
Autonomous unforced L conserves this function.

cards.definition: Nonconservative generalized forces enter Lagrange's equations as Q_j on the right side when those forces are not already represented in L. Including the same force in both the Lagrangian and Q_j double-counts it.
major_error_concepts: Adding a conservative force again as Q after already including its potential.
cards.prompt: What is Nonconservative Generalized Forces? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: External generalized-force term beyond interactions encoded in L.

cards.definition: A velocity-dependent generalized potential can encode certain forces through derivatives with respect to coordinates and velocities. Its presence changes canonical momentum, so the simple identification of momentum with m v can fail.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every force must come from minus the gradient of a position-only scalar potential.
cards.prompt: What is Velocity-Dependent Potential? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Generalized interaction depends on velocity.
Canonical momentum acquires interaction contributions.

cards.definition: For suitable linear viscous damping, a Rayleigh dissipation function R quadratic in generalized velocities gives dissipative force Q_j=-partial R/partial qdot_j. It supplements the equations rather than being a general potential energy for all friction.
major_error_concepts: Treating R as stored potential energy or assuming it covers every friction law unchanged.
cards.prompt: What is Rayleigh Dissipation Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Velocity derivative of R gives negative dissipative force.
Applicable damping class is limited.

cards.definition: Lagrange multipliers can enforce independent holonomic constraints while retaining redundant coordinates in the equations. Their values encode constraint-force contributions with signs and normalization determined by the constraint convention.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a multiplier numerically equals a physical force without checking the constraint's units and normalization.
cards.prompt: What is Constraint Multipliers? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Multipliers enforce constraints and represent reaction contributions.

cards.definition: The Hamiltonian is H(q,p,t)=sum p_j qdot_j-L after velocities are expressed in terms of coordinates and momenta when that inversion is valid. It generates canonical time evolution and need not always equal physical kinetic plus potential energy.
major_error_concepts: Treating H as a function of independent qdot and p after the Legendre transformation is completed.
cards.prompt: What is Hamiltonian? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Legendre-transformed Lagrangian with velocities eliminated.
Physical energy identification is conditional.

cards.definition: A regular Legendre transformation exchanges velocity variables for conjugate momenta when the velocity-to-momentum relation is locally invertible. A singular velocity Hessian can require constrained Hamiltonian treatment instead of naive inversion.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the transformation is invertible for every Lagrangian regardless of degeneracy.
cards.prompt: What is Legendre Transformation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Exchange velocities for momenta through invertible derivative map.

cards.definition: Hamilton's equations are qdot_j=partial H/partial p_j and pdot_j=-partial H/partial q_j in canonical coordinates. They form first-order evolution equations for the coordinate-momentum pairs.
major_error_concepts: Using a positive sign for both canonical derivatives.
cards.prompt: What is Hamilton Equations? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Correct canonical derivative equations and signs.

cards.definition: Phase space records coordinates and conjugate momenta together, typically giving dimension 2n for a regular n-degree-of-freedom system. A point specifies a dynamical state rather than merely a spatial position.
major_error_concepts: Equating phase space with ordinary three-dimensional physical space for every system.
cards.prompt: What is Phase Space? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Coordinate-momentum state space.

cards.definition: The canonical Poisson bracket is {f,g}=sum(f_q g_p-f_p g_q). Hamiltonian evolution gives df/dt={f,H}+partial f/partial t with this convention, linking brackets to conserved observables.
major_error_concepts: Reversing bracket order without changing the sign in the evolution equation.
cards.prompt: What is Poisson Bracket? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Antisymmetric coordinate-momentum derivative bracket.
Correct evolution convention.

cards.definition: A canonical transformation preserves the canonical Hamiltonian structure, equivalently the relevant symplectic form or canonical Poisson-bracket relations. It is more restrictive than an arbitrary invertible relabeling of phase-space coordinates.
major_error_concepts: Calling every invertible phase-space transformation canonical.
cards.prompt: What is Canonical Transformation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Preserve canonical symplectic or bracket structure.

cards.definition: Liouville's theorem states that Hamiltonian flow preserves canonical phase-space volume under the usual smooth regular conditions. It concerns phase-space volume, not necessarily physical-space volume or every projected distribution.
major_error_concepts: Inferring that a Hamiltonian trajectory cannot stretch or fold a phase-space region.
cards.prompt: What is Liouville Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Hamiltonian phase-space volume preservation.

cards.definition: The Hamilton-Jacobi equation is partial S/partial t+H(q,partial S/partial q,t)=0. A suitable complete solution encodes trajectories through an action function and can simplify integrable Hamiltonian motion.
major_error_concepts: Treating an arbitrary scalar function as a Hamilton-Jacobi solution without satisfying the PDE.
cards.prompt: What is Hamilton-Jacobi Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: H evaluated with p=partial S/partial q.
Correct time-derivative equation.

cards.definition: Action-angle variables describe suitable integrable bound motion using constant actions and advancing angles. With the common convention J=(1/2pi) integral p dq around a periodic cycle, the frequency follows from the action dependence of H.
major_error_concepts: Assuming global action-angle variables exist for every chaotic Hamiltonian system.
cards.prompt: What is Action-Angle Variables? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Actions conserved and angles evolve in integrable motion.
Normalization convention stated.

cards.definition: Near an equilibrium, a smooth potential expands as U_0 plus one-half eta transpose K eta to leading nonconstant order when its gradient vanishes. The Hessian K determines local restoring curvature; zero directions may require higher-order terms.
major_error_concepts: Keeping a nonzero linear term while declaring expansion about an unconstrained equilibrium.
cards.prompt: What is Quadratic Potential Expansion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Quadratic potential from Hessian at equilibrium.
Zero curvature needs further terms.

cards.definition: In small-oscillation coordinates, the kinetic energy is one-half etadot transpose M etadot to leading order, where M is the mass matrix at equilibrium. For ordinary independent massive coordinates it is symmetric positive definite.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the mass matrix must be the identity for all generalized coordinates.
cards.prompt: What is Mass Matrix? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Quadratic kinetic-energy coefficient matrix.

cards.definition: The stiffness matrix is the potential Hessian at equilibrium in a small-oscillation model. Its quadratic form measures leading changes in potential energy, with stability interpreted together with allowed directions and the mass matrix.
major_error_concepts: Equating each arbitrary-coordinate diagonal entry alone with an independent mode frequency squared.
cards.prompt: What is Stiffness Matrix? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Potential-curvature matrix.

cards.definition: Small-oscillation modes satisfy K a=omega squared M a. The eigenvectors give collective displacement patterns and eigenvalues give squared frequencies under stable conservative assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Computing frequencies from K alone when the mass matrix is nontrivial.
cards.prompt: What is Small-Oscillation Eigenvalue Problem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Generalized eigenproblem includes both K and M.

cards.definition: For symmetric stiffness and positive-definite mass matrices, distinct-frequency mode vectors are orthogonal under the mass-weighted inner product a transpose M b. Euclidean orthogonality of raw generalized-coordinate vectors is not required.
major_error_concepts: Demanding ordinary component dot products vanish in every nonnormalized coordinate system.
cards.prompt: What is Mass-Weighted Mode Orthogonality? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Distinct modes orthogonal in the M inner product.

cards.definition: Normal coordinates express the motion as a sum of mode patterns and decouple a suitable linear conservative small-oscillation system. Each coordinate then obeys its own oscillator equation with its mode frequency.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the same coordinates exactly decouple arbitrary large nonlinear motion.
cards.prompt: What is Normal Coordinates? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Modal coordinate change decouples the linearized system.

cards.definition: Mode degeneracy means distinct independent mode shapes share the same frequency. Any suitable basis in the degenerate eigenspace describes the same linear mode subspace, and perturbations can split the frequencies.
major_error_concepts: Assuming repeated frequency means there is only one independent mode shape.
cards.prompt: What is Mode Degeneracy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Multiple independent modes with one frequency.

cards.definition: Beats arise when nearby-frequency oscillations superpose, producing a slowly varying amplitude envelope. The beat rate is the absolute frequency difference under the usual two-sinusoid convention, while the fast oscillation occurs near their mean frequency.
major_error_concepts: Calling the envelope frequency the sum of the two nearby frequencies.
cards.prompt: What is Beats? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Nearby-frequency interference produces envelope modulation.

cards.definition: In an uncoupled conservative normal-mode description, each mode has kinetic plus quadratic potential energy conserved independently. Driving, damping, or nonlinear coupling can transfer energy and invalidate separate modal conservation.
major_error_concepts: Assuming nonlinear coupled modes must conserve each mode's energy separately.
cards.prompt: What is Normal-Mode Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Independent mode energy conservation under uncoupled conservative assumptions.

cards.definition: Modal forcing projects applied generalized forces onto mode coordinates. A force excites a mode according to its overlap with that mode, so frequency matching alone is insufficient when the forcing has zero coupling to the pattern.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every drive at a mode frequency necessarily excites that mode regardless of spatial symmetry.
cards.prompt: What is Modal Forcing? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Project forcing onto mode shape.
Zero overlap can prevent excitation.

cards.definition: Parametric excitation varies a system parameter, such as stiffness, with time rather than adding only an external force. It can amplify motion through instability bands whose locations depend on the modulation model.
major_error_concepts: Treating modulation of stiffness as identical to an additive force at the same frequency.
cards.prompt: What is Parametric Excitation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Time-varying coefficient pumps the system.
Distinct from additive forcing.

cards.definition: The steady response of a linearly damped driven mode depends on the drive frequency, damping, and coupling. Its displacement-response peak need not occur exactly at the undamped natural frequency when damping is appreciable.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every definition of resonance peaks at precisely the undamped natural frequency for arbitrary damping.
cards.prompt: What is Resonant Steady Response? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Response curve depends on damping and forcing frequency.

cards.definition: A central force points along the separation from a fixed center and has a magnitude depending only on that separation in the usual conservative central-force model. Its spherical symmetry constrains torque and orbit geometry.
major_error_concepts: Calling any force directed toward a moving arbitrary point a time-independent central potential without further assumptions.
cards.prompt: What is Central Force? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Radial direction and separation-dependent magnitude.

cards.definition: A central force has zero torque about its force center because r cross F is zero. Angular momentum about that center is consequently conserved when no additional torque or moving-origin correction intervenes.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the same zero torque automatically holds about every unrelated origin.
cards.prompt: What is Central-Force Torque? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Parallel r and F give zero torque.
Conservation about the specified center.

cards.definition: The reduced mass of two bodies is mu=m_1 m_2/(m_1+m_2). It is the inertial coefficient for relative motion after center-of-mass motion is separated, not the total mass of the pair.
major_error_concepts: Using the sum of masses as reduced mass.
cards.prompt: What is Reduced Mass? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Correct reduced-mass formula and relative-motion role.

cards.definition: For two constant masses, kinetic energy separates into center-of-mass translation plus one-half mu times relative-speed squared. If the interaction depends only on separation, internal dynamics can be analyzed independently of free center-of-mass motion.
major_error_concepts: Dropping center-of-mass kinetic energy while claiming to report total energy in every frame.
cards.prompt: What is Center-of-Mass Separation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Separate total translation from relative kinetic energy.

cards.definition: With nonzero conserved angular momentum under a central force, relative motion remains in the plane perpendicular to that momentum vector. Zero-angular-momentum motion is the special radial case, not a uniquely determined orbital plane.
major_error_concepts: Claiming zero angular momentum selects a unique normal direction.
cards.prompt: What is Planar Central-Force Motion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Orbit lies in plane normal to conserved angular momentum.
Radial zero-L case is distinct.

cards.definition: Central-force relative motion obeys E=one-half mu rdot squared+U(r)+L squared/(2 mu r squared). The angular term forms part of the effective potential, with mu replacing the single-particle mass in a reduced two-body problem.
major_error_concepts: Using total two-body mass in the angular barrier after reducing to relative coordinates.
cards.prompt: What is Radial Energy Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Radial kinetic plus potential plus angular barrier.

cards.definition: A radial turning point has rdot=0, so the radial energy equals the effective potential there. It reverses radial motion when the surrounding allowed region and force permit; it need not mean zero tangential speed.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the particle is momentarily at rest at every radial turning point.
cards.prompt: What is Radial Turning Point? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: E equals effective potential with zero radial speed.

cards.definition: A circular central-force orbit sits at a stationary point of the effective potential, with radial speed zero and matching energy. This balances the inward force against the angular-motion requirement for the specified angular momentum.
major_error_concepts: Using U prime=0 alone instead of the effective-potential derivative for a nonzero-angular-momentum circular orbit.
cards.prompt: What is Circular-Orbit Condition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Zero effective-potential derivative and zero radial velocity.

cards.definition: A circular orbit is radially stable to small perturbations when the effective potential has positive curvature there, under the usual smooth reduced model. The small radial frequency squared is that curvature divided by reduced mass.
major_error_concepts: Assessing orbital radial stability using only the bare potential curvature while omitting the angular barrier.
cards.prompt: What is Radial Orbital Stability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Positive effective-potential curvature gives radial stability.

cards.definition: For a central radial force F(r), defining u=1/r gives the orbit equation u double prime+u=-mu F(1/u)/(L squared u squared), with primes taken in polar angle. The formula assumes nonzero conserved angular momentum and a stated outward-positive force convention.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting the primes as time derivatives in the stated formula.
cards.prompt: What is Binet Orbit Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Inverse-radius angular orbit equation.
Nonzero L and force-sign convention.

cards.definition: For an attractive inverse-square force, noncollisional Newtonian relative orbits are conic sections with the force center at a focus. Bound negative-energy trajectories are ellipses under the standard zero-at-infinity energy convention.
major_error_concepts: Putting the force center at the geometric center of every eccentric ellipse.
cards.prompt: What is Kepler Conic Orbit? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Inverse-square trajectories are conics with center at focus.

cards.definition: Eccentricity measures conic shape: e=0 is circular, 0<e<1 elliptical, e=1 parabolic, and e>1 hyperbolic for ordinary nondegenerate Kepler conics. Degenerate radial limits require separate care.
major_error_concepts: Calling e greater than one an ordinary bound elliptical orbit.
cards.prompt: What is Orbital Eccentricity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Correct conic classification by eccentricity.

cards.definition: For U=-k/r with k positive and zero potential at infinity, a bound elliptical relative orbit has energy E=-k/(2a), where a is the relative ellipse's semimajor axis. Zero and positive energies correspond to parabolic and hyperbolic escape cases when nondegenerate.
major_error_concepts: Changing the potential zero while applying the same sign classification without adjustment.
cards.prompt: What is Kepler Orbital Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Negative bound energy with E=-k/(2a).
Energy sign uses the stated zero convention.

cards.definition: Areal velocity is the area swept by the radius vector per unit time. In planar central-force motion it is constant and equals L/(2 mu) in the reduced two-body description.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting equal swept areas as equal arc lengths on an eccentric orbit.
cards.prompt: What is Areal Velocity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Swept area rate equals L/(2mu).
Constancy follows from angular-momentum conservation.

cards.definition: For a gravitational two-body ellipse, T squared=4pi squared a cubed/[G(m_1+m_2)], where a is the semimajor axis of relative separation. Using a single body's barycentric semimajor axis without conversion changes the formula.
major_error_concepts: Using reduced mass instead of total mass in the gravitational period denominator.
cards.prompt: What is Kepler Period Relation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Period squared proportional to relative semimajor axis cubed.
Total gravitating mass in denominator.

cards.definition: Classical scattering studies how an incoming trajectory changes direction or state through an interaction. A prediction specifies the potential, incoming conditions, reference frame, and outgoing observable rather than only an interaction label.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a scattering angle is frame-independent without checking the transformation.
cards.prompt: What is Classical Scattering? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Map incoming conditions to outgoing trajectory observables.

cards.definition: The impact parameter is the perpendicular offset of the incoming asymptotic straight-line trajectory from the scattering center. It labels incoming geometry and relates to angular momentum through L=mu v_infinity b for the standard central-force setup.
major_error_concepts: Equating impact parameter with closest-approach distance after deflection.
cards.prompt: What is Impact Parameter? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Incoming transverse offset.
L=mu v_infinity b under stated asymptotic setup.

cards.definition: The scattering angle compares incoming and outgoing asymptotic directions under a specified convention. It is determined by the interaction and incoming state, and may differ between laboratory and center-of-mass frames.
major_error_concepts: Using a laboratory-frame angle as a center-of-mass angle without transformation.
cards.prompt: What is Scattering Angle? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Angle between defined asymptotic trajectory directions.

cards.definition: A differential cross section measures the effective incident area producing outgoing events per unit solid angle. For azimuthally symmetric classical scattering with a single monotonic branch, d sigma/d Omega=b/sin theta times |db/dtheta|; multiple branches contribute additively.
major_error_concepts: Dropping the absolute Jacobian or additional trajectory branches when they are present.
cards.prompt: What is Differential Scattering Cross Section? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Area per outgoing solid angle.
Jacobian and branch assumptions matter.

cards.definition: The center-of-mass collision frame moves so total system momentum is zero for an isolated pair. Transforming to it simplifies relative scattering, but outgoing velocities must be transformed back for laboratory observables.
major_error_concepts: Assuming one particle is at rest in the center-of-mass frame for arbitrary incoming masses and velocities.
cards.prompt: What is Center-of-Mass Collision Frame? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Frame with zero total momentum.
Laboratory observables require inverse transformation.

cards.definition: A rigid body's orientation specifies how its body-fixed axes are related to space-fixed axes. Three local parameters suffice in three dimensions, but common angle coordinates can have singularities and finite rotations do not generally commute.
major_error_concepts: Assuming finite rotations about different axes can always be exchanged in order.
cards.prompt: What is Rigid-Body Orientation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Relation between body and spatial frames.
Three local orientation parameters with possible coordinate singularities.

cards.definition: A proper three-dimensional rotation matrix is orthogonal with determinant plus one. It maps orientation-preserving vector components or active vectors according to the chosen convention, while determinant minus one represents an improper transformation.
major_error_concepts: Calling every orthogonal matrix a proper rotation regardless of determinant.
cards.prompt: What is Rotation Matrix? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Orthogonal matrix with determinant +1.

cards.definition: For a vector fixed in a rotating body, its inertial time derivative is omega cross that vector. Angular velocity describes instantaneous rotation and is not generally the simple vector of three Euler-angle time derivatives.
major_error_concepts: Equating angular-velocity components with arbitrary orientation-angle derivatives without the coordinate relation.
cards.prompt: What is Angular-Velocity Kinematics? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Derivative of body-fixed vector equals omega cross vector.

cards.definition: The inertia tensor about an origin is I_ab=integral(r squared delta_ab-r_a r_b) dm. It is symmetric and relates rigid-body angular velocity to angular momentum for rotation about the specified fixed point or center of mass.
major_error_concepts: Using an inertia tensor about one origin with angular momentum defined about another without translation corrections.
cards.prompt: What is Inertia Tensor? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Correct mass-distribution tensor and origin dependence.

cards.definition: Principal axes are orthogonal eigenvector directions of the inertia tensor, in which its matrix is diagonal. Their eigenvalues are principal moments of inertia, with nonunique axis choices possible in degenerate eigenspaces.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every body's principal axes coincide with arbitrary laboratory coordinate axes.
cards.prompt: What is Principal Axes? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Inertia eigenvectors diagonalize rotational inertia.

cards.definition: For rigid rotation about the relevant fixed point or center of mass, angular momentum is L=I omega. L need not be parallel to omega unless the angular velocity lies along a principal axis or an appropriate degenerate subspace.
major_error_concepts: Using a single scalar I for arbitrary three-axis rotation without specifying an axis.
cards.prompt: What is Rigid-Body Angular Momentum? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Tensor relation L=I omega.
Parallelism is conditional.

cards.definition: Rotational kinetic energy is one-half omega dot I omega about the applicable fixed point or center of mass. Total rigid-body energy includes separate center-of-mass translational kinetic energy when that point moves.
major_error_concepts: Omitting center-of-mass translation while reporting the total kinetic energy of a moving body.
cards.prompt: What is General Rotational Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Quadratic inertia-tensor energy.
Add translation when required.

cards.definition: Euler's rigid-body equations express torque in body axes as tau=(dL/dt)_body+omega cross L. In principal axes this yields coupled equations involving the principal moments, and torque components must use the same frame.
major_error_concepts: Dropping the frame-rotation term for a changing angular-momentum direction in body coordinates.
cards.prompt: What is Euler Rigid-Body Equations? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Body derivative plus omega cross L equals torque.

cards.definition: In torque-free rigid-body motion, angular momentum is fixed in inertial space and rotational kinetic energy is conserved. The body axes and angular velocity can still change direction, especially for unequal principal moments.
major_error_concepts: Assuming zero torque guarantees constant body-axis components of angular momentum.
cards.prompt: What is Torque-Free Rotation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Constant inertial L and rotational energy.
Orientation and omega need not be fixed.

cards.definition: For a torque-free rigid body with three distinct principal moments, steady rotation about the largest or smallest principal axis is stable to small perturbations, while the intermediate-axis rotation is unstable. This is a stability statement around those ideal rotations.
major_error_concepts: Claiming all principal-axis rotations have identical perturbation stability.
cards.prompt: What is Intermediate-Axis Instability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Intermediate principal axis unstable; extremal axes locally stable.

cards.definition: A gyroscope is a rotating system whose angular momentum influences its response to applied torque. Torque changes the angular-momentum vector, which can produce precession instead of motion simply in the torque's intuitive spatial direction.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a spinning gyroscope experiences no gravity or torque.
cards.prompt: What is Gyroscope? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Torque changes a spinning system's angular-momentum vector.

cards.definition: In the slow steady-precession approximation for a rapidly spinning supported symmetric top, the precession rate is approximately M g l/L_spin. The result assumes the relevant torque geometry and a regime where spin angular momentum dominates.
major_error_concepts: Using the simple precession formula as exact for arbitrary top motion and spin rate.
cards.prompt: What is Steady Precession? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Approximate precession rate torque scale divided by spin angular momentum.
Fast-spin steady-precession assumptions.

accepted_variants: Wobbling tilt motion of a top.
cards.definition: Nutation is oscillation of a rotating body's tilt angle superimposed on its other orientation changes, such as precession and spin. It depends on initial conditions and dynamics rather than occurring with one universal amplitude.
major_error_concepts: Equating nutation with steady azimuthal precession at fixed tilt.
cards.prompt: What is Nutation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Oscillatory change in tilt angle.

cards.definition: For any vector A, its inertial derivative equals its rotating-frame derivative plus Omega cross A. Applying this rule twice to position yields the rotational inertial acceleration terms with a consistent frame convention.
major_error_concepts: Reversing frame interpretation without changing the rotational term's sign.
cards.prompt: What is Rotating-Frame Derivative Rule? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Inertial derivative=rotating derivative+Omega cross A.

cards.definition: An angularly accelerating reference frame introduces the Euler inertial force -m Omega dot cross r, where Omega dot is the frame's angular acceleration. It is distinct from centrifugal and Coriolis terms and vanishes for constant Omega.
major_error_concepts: Including an Euler force in uniform rotation solely because Omega is nonzero.
cards.prompt: What is Euler Inertial Force? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Negative mass times angular-acceleration cross position.

accepted_variants: Apparent gravitational acceleration in a rotating frame.
cards.definition: Effective gravity in a steadily rotating frame combines gravitational acceleration with the centrifugal acceleration appropriate to that frame. It differs from the gravitational field alone and depends on location relative to the rotation axis.
major_error_concepts: Adding Coriolis acceleration to a stationary object's effective gravity when its relative velocity is zero.
cards.prompt: What is Effective Gravity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Gravity plus rotating-frame centrifugal contribution.

cards.definition: The ideal plane pendulum obeys theta double prime+(g/l)sin theta=0. Replacing sin theta by theta gives the small-angle harmonic model; at larger oscillation amplitudes the period depends on amplitude.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the small-angle period is exactly amplitude-independent for arbitrarily large librations.
cards.prompt: What is Nonlinear Pendulum? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Nonlinear sine restoring equation.
Small-angle approximation has limited range.

cards.definition: A phase portrait depicts trajectories in a system's state space, such as position-velocity space for one second-order equation. It emphasizes qualitative motion and invariant structures rather than a graph of position against time alone.
major_error_concepts: Calling a simple position-versus-time plot a complete phase portrait.
cards.prompt: What is Phase Portrait? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Trajectories in state space.

cards.definition: A dynamical fixed point is a state where the autonomous evolution vector field vanishes. It represents a constant state in those variables, and its stability requires examining nearby trajectories rather than only solving the equilibrium equation.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every fixed point attracts nearby trajectories.
cards.prompt: What is Dynamical Fixed Point? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Zero state-space velocity in an autonomous system.
Existence does not establish stability.

accepted_variants: A Hurwitz Jacobian gives local asymptotic stability; one growing eigenmode gives instability; purely marginal linear modes need more analysis.
cards.definition: For a smooth continuous-time autonomous system x_dot=F(x), linearize at a fixed point using the Jacobian. If every eigenvalue has strictly negative real part, the equilibrium is locally asymptotically stable. If at least one eigenvalue has strictly positive real part, it is unstable. If none has positive real part but some have zero real part, linearization alone is generally inconclusive for the nonlinear system. These real-part criteria are for differential equations, not discrete-time maps.
major_error_concepts: Calling a saddle stable because one eigenvalue has negative real part.
Declaring nonlinear asymptotic stability from purely imaginary eigenvalues alone.
cards.prompt: What is Linear Stability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: For a smooth continuous-time autonomous system, all fixed-point Jacobian eigenvalues must have strictly negative real parts for the standard asymptotic-stability conclusion.
Any positive-real-part eigenvalue implies instability; a remaining zero-real-part case may require nonlinear analysis.

cards.definition: A separatrix is a trajectory or invariant boundary separating qualitatively different motion types in phase space. For an ideal pendulum it divides oscillations from full rotations at the critical energy, excluding special endpoint interpretations as needed.
major_error_concepts: Treating a separatrix as an arbitrary plotting boundary unrelated to the dynamics.
cards.prompt: What is Separatrix? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Boundary between qualitatively different dynamical regions.

cards.definition: A Duffing oscillator includes a cubic restoring term in addition to linear restoring dynamics, commonly with damping and driving. Its amplitude-dependent behavior can differ from a harmonic oscillator; chaos is possible in suitable driven regimes, not automatic from the cubic term alone.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every unforced conservative cubic oscillator is chaotic.
cards.prompt: What is Duffing Oscillator? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Cubic restoring nonlinearity.
Behavior depends on damping, forcing, and parameters.

cards.definition: A limit cycle is an isolated closed trajectory of an autonomous dynamical system. It may attract or repel nearby trajectories; a continuous family of closed conservative orbits is not an isolated limit cycle.
major_error_concepts: Calling every energy contour of an undamped harmonic oscillator an attracting limit cycle.
cards.prompt: What is Limit Cycle? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Isolated periodic orbit.
Not every closed orbit is a limit cycle.

cards.definition: Deterministic chaos describes aperiodic motion with sensitive dependence on initial conditions in a deterministic system, under an appropriate invariant-set setting. It differs from random forcing and does not mean equations cease to determine evolution.
major_error_concepts: Assuming irregular-looking motion alone proves chaos.
cards.prompt: What is Deterministic Chaos? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Deterministic aperiodic sensitive dynamics.
Not identical to stochastic noise.

cards.definition: A Lyapunov exponent measures an asymptotic exponential rate of separation or contraction of nearby trajectories along a direction. A positive largest exponent supports sensitive dependence in suitable settings, while finite-time estimates depend on duration and method.
major_error_concepts: Treating any brief transient separation as a definitive positive asymptotic Lyapunov exponent.
cards.prompt: What is Lyapunov Exponent? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Exponential perturbation-growth rate.
Finite-time estimates are not automatically asymptotic proof.

cards.definition: A Poincare section records repeated intersections of trajectories with a chosen lower-dimensional surface, with a specified crossing direction. It reveals periodic or more complex structure without retaining every point of the continuous trajectory.
major_error_concepts: Mixing both crossing directions while interpreting a one-direction return map.
cards.prompt: What is Poincare Section? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Repeated directed crossings of a section.

cards.definition: A symplectic integrator preserves the discrete counterpart of Hamiltonian symplectic structure. It often gives useful long-time conservative behavior, but does not generally conserve the exact original energy at every step.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a symplectic method gives exact trajectories or exact energy at arbitrary step size.
cards.prompt: What is Symplectic Integrator? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Preserves symplectic structure.
Not exact energy conservation in general.

cards.definition: Conserved quantities such as energy and momentum provide diagnostic checks on a numerical mechanical trajectory when the modeled conditions imply conservation. Small invariant error is useful but does not alone prove the entire trajectory or implementation correct.
major_error_concepts: Demanding mechanical energy conservation for an explicitly driven dissipative subsystem without accounting for transfers.
cards.prompt: What is Numerical Conservation Diagnostics? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Use applicable invariants as numerical diagnostics.
Necessary evidence is not complete correctness proof.

cards.definition: Mechanical perturbation theory approximates dynamics relative to a simpler solvable system using a small dimensionless parameter. The time interval and possible resonant or secular growth determine whether a nominally small correction remains small.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a small initial correction remains uniformly small for arbitrarily long time.
cards.prompt: What is Mechanical Perturbation Theory? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Small-parameter correction to solvable dynamics.
Validity can depend on elapsed time.

cards.definition: Averaging replaces rapidly oscillating contributions with effective slow evolution when a justified separation of time scales exists. It suppresses detailed fast motion and can fail near resonances or boundaries where the separation breaks down.
major_error_concepts: Averaging away a resonant contribution simply because it oscillates in one representation.
cards.prompt: What is Averaging Method? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Derive slow dynamics by averaging fast variation.
Requires time-scale separation.

cards.definition: An adiabatic invariant is approximately conserved when system parameters vary slowly relative to the relevant internal motion under suitable regularity. For integrable periodic motion, action variables often play this role, but separatrix crossing can invalidate the approximation.
major_error_concepts: Equating adiabatic invariance with exact conservation for arbitrary parameter changes.
cards.prompt: What is Adiabatic Invariant? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Approximate conservation under sufficiently slow variation.
Separatrices and lost scale separation limit it.

cards.definition: Constraint reactions can be recovered from multiplier equations or from Newtonian force balance after the constrained trajectory is known. Eliminating constrained coordinates simplifies motion equations but can hide the forces needed to maintain the constraints.
major_error_concepts: Assuming elimination of a constraint from coordinates means its physical reaction force is zero.
cards.prompt: What is Recovering Constraint Reactions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Recover reactions after or during constrained dynamics.
Reduced coordinates can conceal reaction forces.

cards.definition: Mechanical momentum describes the mass-velocity motion, while canonical momentum is the velocity derivative of the Lagrangian. They can differ through coordinates or velocity-dependent interactions, so conservation of one must not be transferred to the other automatically.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a cyclic-coordinate conserved canonical momentum always equals an unchanged Cartesian m v component.
cards.prompt: What is Canonical and Mechanical Momentum? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: m v versus partial L/partial qdot.
Equality and conservation depend on model.

cards.definition: For a standard time-independent natural Lagrangian with a quadratic kinetic energy and position-only potential in fixed coordinates, H equals T+U. Time-dependent coordinate changes or more general interactions can alter that identification even though Hamilton's equations remain meaningful.
major_error_concepts: Declaring every Hamiltonian automatically equals ordinary kinetic plus potential energy.
cards.prompt: What is Hamiltonian and Physical Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: H=T+U under stated natural-Lagrangian assumptions.
General Hamiltonians need not equal physical energy.

cards.definition: Explicit time dependence in a mechanical model can represent energy exchange through moving constraints or applied drives. The subsystem's energy need not be conserved even when a larger autonomous model could include the driving apparatus and restore total accounting.
major_error_concepts: Calling a driven subsystem's changing energy a violation of total energy conservation without considering the source.
cards.prompt: What is Explicit Time Dependence and Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Time-dependent external conditions can exchange subsystem energy.
System boundary matters.
